newsitem.title: USA: Battle brewing over new U.S. airline taxes.
newsitem.headline: Battle brewing over new U.S. airline taxes.

text.p: With the federal airline ticket tax now expired, a battle is brewing over how Congress should fashion a new method to raise money for air traffic control and other aviation needs.

A coalition of the seven major airlines is lined up against smaller, low-cost carriers over whether the 10 percent tax on tickets should be reimposed or whether money should be raised in other ways, including user fees.
The tax, which had gone into a fund to finance Federal Aviation Administration operations, expired on Dec. 31.
FAA officials say fast Congressional action is needed to replenish the fund, which, without new money, will be depleted by some $500 million a month and be depleted by summer.

The big carriers want the 10 percent tax dropped in favour of a user fee they say would be more equitable. The fee would be based on the size of aircraft, the number of passengers flown and distance travelled.
Scott Yohe, a senior vice president of Delta Air Lines Inc., one of coalition members, said, "This system is much fairer."
With the 10 percent tax, the coalition said, passengers on the big airlines are subsidising the low-cost airlines.

But Southwest Airlines Co. spokeswoman Linda Rutherford disputed the argument that the 10 percent tax was unfair, saying big carriers use the air traffic control system as heavily or more heavily than do the smaller carriers.

She said low-cost airline point-to-point flights take far less air traffic controller time than the big carriers with hub and spoke operations that often have many planes landing, taking off and on the ground at the same time.
"We believe a flat tax is the most equitable way to fund the FAA," Rutherford said.

The tax lapsed last year when a bill that included it was vetoed by President Clinton, but it was reimposed several months ago as an interim funding effort while Congress studied longer term methods to finance FAA operations.
While the FAA would like a fast reinstatement, some Congressional observers see no move until two panels finish their studies on taxes and fees and make recommendations.

One is a House of Representatives Task Force that is studying all federal transportation taxes and the other is a National Aviation Review Commission that is looking into using a fee system instead of taxes to pay for the FAA services.
Their reports are due early this year.
Yohe said the coalition would like a user fee based on specific FAA costs.
For example, he said, a carrier flying between Atlanta and Washington would be assessed a fee to cover the actual cost of FAA air traffic control services used for that flight.
As another example, he said, Boeing would pay the FAA for the agency's cost of certifying its new aircraft.
The coalition said the 10 percent tax was imposed in the 1970s and made sense when airlines were regulated and fares were essentially the same in each market.

But now, it said, with deregulation, ticket prices vary widely, even on the same flight, and so passengers on different airlines and even on the same plane pay different amounts for the same FAA services.
"The air traffic control system benefits all passengers regardless of how much they pay to travel," the big airlines said. "It is time to put an end to the ticket tax. It is time for a user fee."
But Southwest's Rutherford said that if the big carriers wanted to reduce the ticket tax they collect, they could reduce their fares.
"The fare is completely within their control," she said.
